processes.name: Meter flow without a valid deal: extension, new-deal and write-off requests
processes.description: Volume management, logistics and settlement staff find gas flowing at an HPL meter with no active Sitara deal. The deal may have expired or missed its evergreen roll, the flow may be parked on the Strangers Gas contract, or the meter may be new. They email Daren Farmer, one meter at a time, asking him to extend or roll a deal, create a new one, or sign a printed write-off to Unaccounted for Gas. Allocation, accounting arrangements and invoicing cannot go ahead until he answers. This is the largest and most frequent process in the archive. Nearly every batch shows it, and almost all of it runs through one person.
processes.stall_points: Every request waits on Daren Farmer, who is also trading, so requesters send reminders and the same meters come back the next month. Write-offs need a printed, signed and returned original. Forwarded threads carry long quoted history. Feedback and bridge errors pass through four or five people before reaching the deal owner. Deal numbers are sometimes wrong or sit with another desk, and suspended counterparties or expired contracts block the fix.
processes.automation: A daily and month-end exception job that compares allocated meter flow with active Sitara deals and lists every meter with flow and no deal, including Strangers Gas allocations and lapsed evergreens. Each exception goes to the deal owner as a pre-filled work item with the meter, days, volume and the prior deal proposed for extension, plus one-click options to extend, create or approve a write-off electronically, with status tracking and automatic reminders. This replaces the one-off emails, the printed approval forms and the chasers.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observers' estimates ranged from 15 to 90 minutes. Most clustered at 15 to 25 minutes across requester and approver, so the median of 20 minutes is used. Detection and routing automate well, but the commercial decision to extend, re-deal or write off stays human, so the fraction is held at the median of 0.5.

processes.name: Customer and producer gas nomination intake and re-keying
processes.description: Customers, producers and pipelines send daily, weekend and monthly gas nominations and revisions by email. Examples include Calpine, Enron Methanol and MTBE, KCS Josey Ranch, TXU, Reliant, Valero and Prize Energy, and the nominations usually come as Word or spreadsheet attachments with little body text. Ami Chokshi and other trade-support staff forward them to schedulers. Schedulers re-key the volumes into Sitara, POPS or Unify and ask Daren Farmer to approve revisions, and risk prepares next-month estimates from prior-month noms. Each revision repeats the cycle, so the same customer can generate several rounds a month.
processes.stall_points: Attachments arrive with blank subjects and no body text and are forwarded by hand. Each file has to be opened and re-keyed, and entry mistakes creep in. Revisions need Daren's approval before anything changes. Nominations sometimes arrive before the transport contract or meter number exists, and unresponsive producers have to be chased against deadlines. Estimates are sent in fragments.
processes.automation: A nomination ingestion service that reads the nomination emails and attachments into structured rows (counterparty, meter, day, volume). It diffs each row against the current Sitara and POPS volumes, posts only the changes to the scheduling queue for one-click approval, and auto-acknowledges the sender when nothing changed. It also proposes next-month estimates and swing volumes from prior-month and prior-year flow. This replaces the manual forwarding, re-keying and approval emails.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer estimates ran from 10 to 30 minutes, with a median of 15 minutes per nomination or revision including forwarding, keying and approval. Parsing and diffing structured attachments is highly automatable, but judgement on swings and revisions remains, so the fraction is set at the 0.5 median.

processes.name: Gas invoice and deal price discrepancy resolution
processes.description: Settlements and accounting staff compare counterparty invoices, statements and payment claims with Sitara and Unify. They find price differences, missing days, wrong counterparties or one-sided deals, then email the deal owner (Daren Farmer, Julie Meyers) to confirm the right deal and price and to correct the ticket so Unify can be redrafted. The owner often has to ask a trader or the counterparty before answering. Invoice deadlines and counterparty phone calls keep up the pressure while questions bounce between people.
processes.stall_points: Requests sit with one or two deal owners and are re-sent when they are out. Questions bounce between settlements, logistics, measurement and traders for days or weeks, and invoice and payment cut-offs pass. Some disputes run for months, and counterparties call repeatedly. Volume Management sometimes shows no actualized volume, so nobody can confirm the amount.
processes.automation: An automatic invoice-to-deal match that compares each counterparty invoice or statement line with the Sitara deal price, volume, counterparty and entity. Each mismatch is raised as a tracked case routed to the ticket owner, carrying the deal, the invoice line and the allocation already attached. Corrections in Sitara notify settlements automatically so Unify can be redrafted, which replaces the email threads and chasers.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer medians cluster at 25 to 45 minutes, and the message-weighted median is 30 minutes across requester and owner. Matching and routing automate well, but resolving the true price with traders or counterparties does not, so the fraction is set at the 0.4 median.

processes.name: Gas Sitara deal entry, transport and buyback ticket setup requests
processes.description: Producer Services, traders, settlements and logistics email the gas desk (Tom Acton, Daren Farmer, schedulers) to key new spot or well deals into Sitara. Other requests ask to add meters or change points on existing deals, set up monthly transport usage and buyback or swing tickets for industrial customers, book processing-plant deals, or enter one-off sales such as storage. Each request is free text that someone re-types into Sitara, POPS or Unify before replying with the ticket number or a change notice. Rates are kept in both Unify and Sitara and have to be checked by hand each month.
processes.stall_points: Details are re-typed from email, and errors such as a wrong price or missing deal number need a second email. Requesters do not know who owns a deal or has access, so mails bounce between intermediaries. Inactive counterparties or contracts block entry for weeks. Change notices are followed by several correction emails. Transport rates live in two systems and are corrected twice.
processes.automation: A structured deal-request form and queue that validates counterparty, meter, contract status, price and dates, then writes the Sitara ticket draft for one-click approval and returns the ticket number automatically. Monthly transport usage, buyback and swing tickets would roll forward from the prior month, with only rate changes flagged against the rate matrix and Unify. Change notices would be generated from the deal-change log.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer estimates range from 8 to 60 minutes with a median of 30 minutes, reflecting multi-party back-and-forth. Validation and ticket drafting can be automated, but many requests carry pricing or commercial judgement, so the fraction is set at the 0.35 median.

processes.name: Gas volume, imbalance and pathing reconciliation
processes.description: Volume management, logistics and settlement analysts reconcile gas volumes across MOPS, POPS, Sitara, Unify and pipeline statements. They work allocation exceptions, UA4 and zero-volume feed problems, measurement and nomination-versus-flow gaps, production imbalances and intercompany or interdesk variances, and they clear unpathed deals and bridge-back errors before the month-end close cutoff. Transwestern does the equivalent reconciliation with El Paso and other pipelines. Each item is researched by hand and then chased by email to whoever must re-path, reallocate or correct the volume.
processes.stall_points: Fixes need the right person to act in POPS or Unify, and ownership of pipelines and paths is often unclear after reassignments. The same variances come back for weeks. Zero-volume feeds are overridden by hand each night because the system team has not fixed the root cause. Pipeline meter statements arrive by fax on request. Bridge-back errors must be cleared against a hard clock time, and multi-step tasks such as meter replacements wait on each hand-off.
processes.automation: A daily reconciliation job that compares nominated, confirmed, measured and allocated volumes across MOPS, POPS, Sitara, Unify and loaded pipeline statements. It flags zero-feed meters, one-sided intercompany deals, unpathed deals and bridge-back errors, and puts each exception in a shared queue with an owner from a pipeline and zone registry, an age, and automatic reminders ahead of the close cutoff. This replaces manual spreadsheet research and forwarded issue lists.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observers estimated 20 to 120 minutes because items need multi-party research, and the median is 45 minutes. Detection and routing automate well, but root-cause research and counterparty agreement do not, so the fraction is set at the median of about 0.35.

processes.name: Gas pipeline outage, cut and on-call notice relay
processes.description: Gas control, field staff, plant contacts and schedulers email long distribution lists about pipeline maintenance, meter shut-ins, plant upsets, capacity reductions and pipeline cuts. Weekend on-call staff also send narrative notes. Schedulers read each notice, work out which nominations are affected, and decide whether to zero volumes, buy back, cut, or negotiate with the producer. Updates come as repeated forwards that revise earlier notices.
processes.stall_points: Notices are typed by hand and sent to 15 to 40 people. Each reschedule is a new forwarded chain that has to be re-read. The volume decision waits on someone mapping the notice to nominations, and producer notice letters are written by hand. On-call notes are free text or attachments with no body, and cuts are relayed after the fact.
processes.automation: A shared outage and cut log keyed by meter and pipeline, populated from gas control and pipeline notices. It matches each event against open nominations, alerts the owning scheduler with a proposed volume change, auto-generates producer notice letters, and publishes a structured weekend on-call summary. This replaces the free-text broadcast emails and re-forwards.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer estimates range from 10 to 30 minutes per notice across sender and readers, with a median of 20 minutes. Matching and distribution automate well, but the nomination decision remains a judgement call, so the fraction is set at the 0.4 median.

processes.name: Recurring hand-built operational report distribution
processes.description: Several staff rebuild the same recurring report by hand and email it to a fixed list: Kimberly Vaughn's HL&P month-to-date flow spreadsheet, monthly storage and industrial reports, Michelle Lokay's Friday Transwestern California capacity report with Gas Daily prices, and the daily Energy Market Report and Gas and Power Daily PDFs. processes.stall_points: Numbers are compiled and typed by hand every cycle, so late data delays the report. Files are requested from another person each time. Reports are resent with the wrong label or a missing attachment, and distribution list changes are handled by email.
processes.automation: Scheduled report jobs that pull flow, throughput, delivery and price data from the source systems into the standard template, compute derived figures such as shortfalls against tolerance and utilisation, and email a maintained subscription list automatically when the data is published. This replaces manual compilation and forwarding.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer estimates range from 10 minutes for forwarding to 45 minutes for compiling, with a median of about 35 minutes. Most reports follow a fixed template from system data, so the fraction is set high at the 0.65 median.

processes.name: Daily credit report forwarding and counterparty rebook actions
processes.description: Each business day the credit group (Veronica Espinoza, Russell Diamond) emails a Credit Report listing counterparties to rebook and pending credit actions. Darron Giron forwards each one unchanged to a desk analyst (usually Carole Frank), who then performs the TAGG rebooks by hand. When he is out, the reports pile up and are forwarded in a batch days later.
processes.stall_points: This is pure manual pass-along through one person. Reports are forwarded hours or days late and in lumps after absences, which delays the rebook actions. Rebooks are then keyed by hand in TAGG.
processes.automation: Route the credit report automatically to the desk distribution list or shared mailbox when it is sent. Parse its rebook and pending table into a per-desk task list with TAGG deal numbers. This removes the forwarding step entirely.
processes.estimate_rationale: All four observers estimated 3 to 4 minutes per forward with 0.8 to 0.85 automatable. Forwarding is fully mechanical, while the rebook judgement stays human, so 4 minutes and 0.8 are used.

processes.name: Risk book administration: book setup, deal rebooks, book flips and price corrections
processes.description: Darron Giron and the risk book administrators receive a steady flow of requests. Some ask for new trading books, portfolios, curves and mappings in TAGG, Sitara, CPR, TDS and Global Counterparty. Others ask to flip deals between books (for example ECC and Canadian deals to FT-US/CAND-ERMS), rebook counterparties, change deal rates or demand charges, add missing Sitara, TAGG or EOL cross-references, and supply book lists or reference ids. Each request is a separate email that Giron actions himself or forwards to the book owner. Settlements and invoicing often cannot proceed until the change is confirmed.
processes.stall_points: Requests go to several different administrators, and routing is unclear (for example, a TAGG book must first exist in Global Counterparty). Requests arrive piecemeal and urgently for same-day invoicing. Cross-system ids are not linked, so lookups are manual. Recurring monthly rate changes sit unactioned until chased. Book lists are rebuilt for each requester.
processes.automation: One intake form and queue for book, curve and mapping setup that routes to every system's administrator and shows status. A bulk deal-attribute change tool would take a list of deal numbers with the target book or counterparty. A rule would flag deals with Canadian counterparties in US books, and recurring rate changes would load from the monthly price source. Validation at entry would auto-link TAGG, Sitara and EOL ids, and a maintained book and portfolio reference table would serve book lists.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer estimates centre on 15 to 30 minutes with a median of 20 minutes. Most changes are mechanical once approved, so the fraction is set at the 0.5 median.

processes.name: Bankruptcy and Netco separation bulk deal moves
processes.description: After the bankruptcy filings and during the Netco separation, credit, legal and contracts staff repeatedly send spreadsheets of deals or counterparties that must be zeroed, killed or moved into bankruptcy books. The gas risk group (Love, Giron, Gossett) cross-checks each list against the books and sends move requests to IT (Cecilia Cheung), who runs book-move scripts and retranslates. Each move needs its parameters clarified by email.
processes.stall_points: Lists arrive as updates, stragglers and corrections, so versions must be reconciled. Requests lack book ids, commodity code or cutoff date, which forces clarification rounds. The impact on Unify paths is questioned only after thousands of deals are announced for killing.
processes.automation: A master deal-move list that is matched automatically against the books by counterparty and deal id, flagging gaps and duplicates. A parameterised move request would capture source and target book, commodity, cutoff date and Canadian or US logic once, and an impact check would run against Unify paths and volumes before the script executes, with completion sent automatically.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer estimates were 40 to 60 minutes with a median of 45 minutes per list cycle. List matching and parameter capture automate well, but legal and credit decisions on scope stay human, so the fraction is set at 0.5.

processes.name: Daily P&L, DPR, officialization and origination checks
processes.description: Each night the risk book owners run the calc and officialize every post id and basis position. They email the daily P&L and DPR with notes on held-back amounts and UA4, and they send Schedule C add or release notes to credit. They also reconcile origination granted against origination recognised by book. Darron Giron drives most of this for the gas desks, forwarding macros and reminders to his analysts and answering variance emails from P&L analysts. Missed books end up on a daily exception list that goes to senior management.
processes.stall_points: Officializing depends on an admin remembering to do it, and the benchmark check misses books with no net position. Reports go out with the wrong or a missing attachment. Origination grants arrive late, so the same variance is reported again. The calc depends on the system being up. Protected DPR copies have to be re-requested.
processes.automation: A nightly scheduled job that verifies every book and post id is officialized, including zero-position ones, and emails exceptions to each controller. After the calc, it would generate and distribute the daily P&L, DPR and Schedule C amounts automatically, and an automatic origination granted-versus-recognised comparison would flag only residual differences.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer estimates range from 5 to 40 minutes with a median of 20 minutes per daily cycle. Checking, generation and distribution are mechanical, while explaining unusual P&L is not, so the fraction is set at the 0.5 median.

processes.name: Month-end P&L close, valuation and audit support requests
processes.description: At month-end and quarter-end the risk desks close the books: last-day files, economics and OA reviews, P&L restatements and write-off decisions. They also field repeated requests for support. Arthur Andersen asks for P&L top pages and curve shift reports, risk asks for curve validation explanations, accounting asks for liquidation support, and the Confirmations group asks for back-dated MTM valuations for counterparty audits. Darron Giron receives most requests and forwards them to analysts, who rebuild the support by hand each month.
processes.stall_points: Requests arrive as second requests and are forwarded several times. Owners are out and requests go unseen. There is no system with back-dated curves, so a risk person is interrupted for each valuation. Gas accounting cannot start until every desk replies, and errors such as killed January activity are found after close, forcing restatements.
processes.automation: A month-end checklist that tracks desk completion with variance checks on the P&L tabs. Standard extracts for top pages, curve shifts and liquidation support per region would be filed automatically to the shared directory, and a valuation tool with back-dated curves would let Confirmations self-serve MTM. An auditor request tracker would map each desk to its preparer.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer estimates run from 20 to 120 minutes with a median of 45 minutes. Extract generation helps, but much of the work is analysis and explanation, so the fraction is set at the 0.3 median.

processes.stall_points: Few people respond by the deadline, so reminders and new deadlines follow. The same driver numbers are re-keyed every month. This replaces the broadcast emails, attachments and chasers.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer estimates span 4 to 60 minutes, and the median across the merged items is 30 minutes per manager cycle. Prefill and reminders automate a good share, but the content still needs owner judgement, so the fraction is set at the 0.4 median.

processes.name: System access, IT and directory requests
processes.description: Staff request application access, trader IDs, book calc and print rights, TDS approvers, shared ISO logins, equipment, turrets and phones through email or the SRRS ticket system, then follow up when access is partial. During the UBS and Netco transition, IT and desk leads also chased each user for access methods and estate-account exceptions and coordinated database outages. A separate recurring irritant is the name collision between Bill Williams and Bill Williams III, which misroutes mail and access requests that then have to be forwarded and corrected.
processes.stall_points: Requests wait on approvers who are not the right ones. Grants arrive partially and need a second request. Each request triggers several automated emails that must be opened. Users do not answer surveys until chased. Shared credentials circulate by email. Senders keep choosing the wrong Bill Williams, so the same correction is repeated.

processes.name: Meeting, shift and coverage scheduling
processes.description: Assistants, managers and desk leads arrange meetings, training classes, conference calls and travel by email: proposing slots, collecting reply-all availability and re-sending reschedule notices. Desk leads also distribute shift schedules, collect swaps, canvass volunteers for holiday and weather coverage, and send out-of-office notes naming who covers each pipeline or desk. Rosters are compiled by hand from individual replies.
processes.stall_points: Availability is polled reply by reply, and meetings are cancelled and rescheduled with each notice re-sent to the full list. Dial-in details are requested afterwards. Shift swaps must be both emailed and hand-marked on the posted schedule. Coverage notes are free text that the backup has to interpret.
processes.automation: Calendar scheduling with availability polling, invites that carry the agenda and dial-in, and automatic reschedule notices. A shared shift and coverage roster would take swaps and volunteer sign-ups once, notify the manager automatically, and route questions to the named backup when someone is marked out.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer estimates cluster at 10 to 15 minutes with a median of 15 minutes. Standard scheduling tools remove most of the back-and-forth, so the fraction is set at the 0.5 median.

processes.name: Real-time power position hand-off and Enpower/CAPS deal entry
processes.description: On the Portland real-time desk, Bill Williams, prescheduling and the cash desks email the shift whenever the book is short or long. Each email gives MW, hours, hub, price, book and deal numbers, along with instructions for El Paso Electric lending days and EOL trades. Shift traders and support re-key these into Enpower, CAPS and the position sheets, following entry rules that are restated by email. Mismatches between the emailed positions and Enpower are clarified by further emails.
processes.stall_points: Instructions are sent piecemeal and re-forwarded as more trades are made. The same shorts and deal numbers are re-sent day after day. Price and counterparty details are deferred to 'check with' other traders. Emailed positions carry wrong hours, delivery points or deal numbers. Lending prices and deal numbers are re-keyed per day and corrected afterwards, and EOL deals go missing in Enpower.
processes.automation: Generate the shift position summary directly from the position manager and the Enpower deals. Templated deal sets (for example EPE lending) and EOL trades would be auto-created in Enpower with book and strip defaults, and validated against desk rules. A daily match of broker and EOL deals against Enpower would flag gaps, replacing free-text position emails and manual re-keying.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer estimates mostly sit at 8 to 20 minutes per hand-off, with two outliers at 60 and 90 minutes, giving a median of 15 minutes. Position data already sits in systems, so the fraction is set at the 0.5 median.

processes.name: Standing procedure reminders and market notice broadcasts
processes.description: Desk managers broadcast standing rules and market changes to their groups by email. On the real-time power desk these cover CAISO and FERC notices, price caps, path derates, tagging, congestion bidding, time zones and delivery points. In gas risk, Giron forwards Gossett's procedure memos to book administrators, and in gas logistics managers send reminders on EOL deal handling. The same rules are restated after each error because they live only in email.
processes.stall_points: Each notice is forwarded separately to several people, sometimes weeks late or without its attachment. New staff repeat old errors, such as wrong tiered bids, wrong time zones or altered EOL deals, which produces disputes and after-hours re-pathing. Forwarding depends on one person seeing each notice.
processes.automation: Auto-route CAISO and market notices to the desk distribution list with a summary and an acknowledgement tracker. Keep the desk rules on one maintained page, and encode the key rules as validation at deal entry: lock EOL-sourced tickets, check tier bids, time zones and delivery points, and require the physical flag. This replaces repeated broadcast reminders.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer estimates range from 3 to 25 minutes with a median of 10 minutes per notice including reading and correcting. Routing is fully automatable, but interpretation is not, so the fraction is set at about the 0.45 median.

processes.name: Power settlement reconciliation: congestion revenue, PMAs and counterparty disputes
processes.description: The Portland real-time desk hand-calculates CAISO congestion relief revenue and emails it to the flash and settlement group to check against the next morning's flash. Volume Management recalculates it by hour. At month-end, desk heads and support review prior-month adjustments line by line and query mismatches with Settlements. They also reconcile ISO revenue against volume management and work counterparty disputes (El Paso Electric, SRP, MPC), which means requesting trade tapes and reconstructing what happened on specific hours.
processes.stall_points: Amounts are hand-calculated, and hours go missing from both sides' calculations and from the CAISO site. One-sided PMAs, such as revenue reversed with no cost reversed, stay open across several emails. Disputes drag for months, and tape access goes through another person. About 30 disputes arose from EOL deals altered without notes. Sheets go to the wrong recipients.
processes.automation: Compute hourly congestion revenue from CAISO award files and schedules, and reconcile it automatically against the flash, the inc sheet and settlement entries, alerting only on mismatches. PMA lines would be matched to Enpower deal changes so one-sided adjustments are flagged, and a dispute tracker would link each disputed deal to its tape, evidence and decision, with a required reason field on deal alterations.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer estimates run from 15 minutes for flash notes to 90 minutes for month-end PMA and ISO true-ups, with a median of 45 minutes. Calculation and matching automate well, but dispute resolution does not, so the fraction is set at the 0.4 median.

processes.name: Real-time power schedule, cut and variance corrections
processes.description: Real-time shift traders spend part of each day correcting schedules and positions. When Colstrip or a counterparty cuts, they zero deals and book offsetting annuities. They fix import IDs and load zones, create DA and HA finals in CAPS, and run the SAR and INC reconciliation against CAPS and Enpower. They also repair El Paso Electric schedules with missing tags, check out schedules with counterparties by phone, and call generators every hour for checkout. The same cut is recorded in several places, including paper cut sheets and a Lotus Notes database, and procedures are re-issued when entries are inconsistent.
processes.stall_points: Variances are found after the fact and need detective work. Real-time cuts are not in CAPS, so the SAR and INC only match after manual additions. HA finals creation hits SQL errors and data scrape failures that go unnoticed over weekends. The EPE schedule sheet misses tags day after day. Paper cut sheets get lost, and hourly generator calls are sometimes missed.
processes.automation: A cut-entry form that zeroes the deal, books the offsetting annuity and logs the cut once to every destination. An automated morning SAR, INC and CARP comparison would write the reconciliation sheet. Tags in the EPE schedule would be validated automatically against dispatcher schedules, and the scrape and finals imports would be monitored with alerts. Metered generator output would be pulled into the services sheet automatically.
processes.estimate_rationale: Observer estimates cluster at 20 to 45 minutes with a median of 30 minutes per occurrence. Detection and logging are automatable, but resupply and counterparty checkout decisions stay human, so the fraction is set at the 0.45 median.
